abstract: Previous studies (1, 2) have shown that radioactive carbon from uniformly labeled glucose is incorporated in vitro into all of the protein-bound amino acids except proline and threonine by minced 1 day-old mouse brain. Inoculation of such preparations with Theiler's GD VII mouse encephalomyelitis virus resulted in extensive virus propagation and an increased incorporation of radioactivity into all of the labeled amino acids except lysine and histidine. The distribution of radioactivity in the various amino acids was extensive and made difficult the interpretation of the intermediary pathways by which this incorporation may have occurred and the nature of the reactions affected by virus infection. It seemed possible that a study of the incorporation of simpler substrates into the protein-bound amino acids might be more simply interpreted. In the present study, therefore, the extent of incorporation of radioactive carbon from C4-labeled acetate, formate, and bicarbonate into the protein-bound amino acids of mouse brain has been investigated.

abstract: Ouabain in concentrations of from 10-6 to 10-3 M produced a sustained increase in the respiratory rate of cat heart slices. Such a stimulation could only be demonstrated after depression of the original respiratory rate by preincubation or by treatment with barbiturate. When the glycoside was added to undepressed slices the respiration was inhibited by all concentrations of ouabain from 10-6 to 10-3 M. Ouabain had no effect upon the oxidative or phosphorylative capacity of cat heart or guinea pig brain mitochondrial preparations, nor did the drug stimulate such mitochondrial preparations which had been depressed by barbiturate or calcium. The results are interpreted as indicating that the effects of ouabain on intact heart cells are mediated by some other means than a direct action upon oxidative enzymes per se.

abstract: We know many a drug which produces narcosis or excitement on the brain, and is of a great importance both in pharmacology and in clinical practice. However, the chemical basis for the pharmacological action of these neurotropic agents, especially of the convulsants is ill-defined yet.McIlwain(1), Stone(2) and Richter(3) insisted that the lactic acid concentration in the brain serves as a reliable indicator to the change of the function al activity of the brain. Since Quastel(4) postulated that narcotics inhibit the oxidative metabolism in brain tissues, many active investigations have been attempted to clarify how a narcotic acts upon the nervous system. Inspite of those keen attempts for the closer approach we can't be as yet favored with the clear-cut view on that mechanism.Nachmansohn(5) reported that the transmissions of action potential and of impulse in nerve cells are certainly connected with the release and inactivation of the acetylcholine (ACh), the resynthesis of which and the action potential of nerve cells are provided with the energy by energy-rich bonds in the phosphate linkage. According to Dawson(6) the breakdown of acetylcholine complex is likely to be related to the function of nerve cells.The following description of our experimentation designates an attempt to investigate the relationships of acetylcholine, phosphate esters, lactic acid and the functional activity in a certain area of the cerebral cortex where excitement or narcosis is induced by some kinds of neurotropic agents.

abstract: Coma, with its frequently abysmal outcome, is devastating for patients and their families. It is also an immensely costly condition. Thus it is of paramount importance that the physician be able to identify those patients with potentially good outcomes, and conversely to identify those patients in whom additional treatment would be costly and futile. Cheyne's monograph (1812) published almost 190 years ago singled out "the comatose diseases" for special attention, but more recently (at least in the United States), the book by Plum and Posner (1982)- The Diagnosis of Stupor and Coma -has been the leading guide for generations of neurologists. Practicing physicians can gain diagnostic, therapeutic, and prognostic guidance for comatose patients from the large study of Levy et al. (1981) and from the work of Plum and Posner (1982), both of which are based on bedside clinical observations. Particularly in anoxic coma, prognosis has relied substantially on the clinical flow diagrams of Levy et al. (1981), which examine the best outcome for patients retaining some brainstem reflexes, as well as verbal and motor responses. Taking a different approach, there have been other important contributions that have examined the role of EEG (and the classification of the severity of EEG abnormality), the use of brainstem auditory evoked potentials, and shortand long-latency somatosensory evoked potentials to determine outcome. These studies demonstrate that testing patients with impaired brainstem function with brainstem auditory evoked potentials may predict poor outcome. Using EEG and somatosensory evoked potentials, poor outcome may also be predicted even when brainstem reflexes are present. There have been major advances in the prognostication of coma outcome by supplementing clinical neurologic examination with electrophysiologic testing. Only recently, multivariate analyses have included these modalities in an attempt to improve the sensitivity and specificity, as well as to quantify the negative and positive predictive value of these tests, individually and in combination. More tests are in development or becoming available, such as the use of cognitive evoked potentials, positron emission tomography, and single photon emission computed tomography (using hexamethyl propylenamineoxine and xenon), but much work remains to be done to determine the usefulness of these techniques. To date, the major advances in prognosis have been brought about by using EEG and evoked potentials, along with data from the clinical neurologic examination. Despite the consistent demonstration of the value of this "triumvirate" of techniques in the evaluation of coma, there is a perceived lack of physician awareness of their usefulness, especially of EEGs and evoked potentials. To address this deficiency, a symposium on "Coma: The Pathophysiology and the Clinical and Electrophysiologic Determination of Outcome" was held at the annual American Clinical Neurophysiology Society meeting, October 1999, in St. Louis, MO. This special issue of theJournal of Clinical Neurophysiologyis dedicated primarily to this symposium. The presentations herein were adapted from the symposium presentations by the authors, modified in light of the cross-fertilization of ideas derived from the most recent studies of electrophysiology and coma prognosis found in their colleagues' presentations, and supplemented (for some authors) by additional data presented at the Third International Conference on Coma and Brain Death, which took place in Havana, Cuba, in February 2000. The contents are organized to flow from a discussion of the substrates of consciousness, through ethics in the intensive care unit, to particular ethical and practical issues pertinent to pediatric coma. Clinical, EEG, and evoked potential contributions are then developed in separate articles, followed by a meta-analysis of combined study data. The Afterword proposes guidelines for patient investigation and future study. Long underused, and frequently neglected, electrophysiology has a very contemporary and pertinent contribution to make in coma evaluation and prognosis.

abstract: Chairman Perlstein: In neuromuscular disabilities there are many problems to consider. However, about half of these comprise that group of diseases we know as cerebral palsy. We will start by orientating ourselves toward cerebral palsy, and in the discussion taking up the question of differential diagnosis and related subjects. Cerebral palsy is not a single disease but a group of conditions which have in common a disorder of the motor system. It can be paralysis, incoordination, tremors or excessive motions, due to involvement of the motor centers of the brain. In other words, palsy and cerebral are defined. The important thing about cerebral is that the motor centers must be involved. If the problem is lack of development because of mental deficiency, you can exclude it. Likewise, spinal palsy, polio, and other causes of motor defects not due to involvement of the motor center are excluded. In schools for children with physical handicaps of all types, about half the children are cerebral palsied. So, from the viewpoint of frequency, cerebral palsy is the most frequent of the disabling conditions. Much confusion exists in the terminology and classification of cerebral palsy. The term "Little's disease" has often been used as a generic term to cover all forms of cerebral palsy. Actually, Little described only one of the many types. Likewise, the term "spastic" is often used by the doctor and laymen to cover all categories. This tendency is conducive to loose thinking. A logical classification of the types of cerebral palsy would help to clarify this confused subject.
